blocks.x: The
Matters that I'm working on. Were you born here in town?
No, I was born in Mobile, Alabama.
Well, that gets us very close to where an awful lot of our people in the music business come from, don't they? And what was your name before marriage?
Lilidel, D-E-L-K.
I see. And you added the Christian after marriage. And when did you marry Mr. Christian?
You were born in Mobile. You want to give me dates? Doesn't matter.
Huh?
You want to give me the dates? March the 12th.
I don't have to give you the year.
All right. Well, I can guess that. But I can't guess accurately. Mobile, Alabama.
Yeah.
And did you marry in Chicago?
Yeah.
1922, what was the date of marriage? Do you remember?
August the 20th.
August the 20th. What's Mr. Christian's first name? Charlie.
Where'd he come from?
Dallas, Texas. Well, how did you happen to get into Chicago?
Well, my parents moved here.
Oh, well, I don't care. When did they come out?
They moved here. They all moved here. We all moved here in 1915.
Do you have any connection with music before he came to Chicago? Oh, no. It happened long after. No.
Yes, long after. Now, the first of my starting to in the entertainment world was making those records.
Well, somebody must have heard you. You see, well, yes. Just before that or then that.

I tell you, Johnny St. Cyr, he's a very good friend of Louis Armstrong. They all was from New Orleans. Yeah. See? He's dead now. Johnny St. Cyr, he heard me. We were living at that time, 39, 38 Indiana Avenue. That was around 25, 24, 25, like that. So I recorded a couple of records with him, you know, first. And then he spoke to Louis about me. And then Louis, I'm sorry this thing is broke. I'd like for you to hear. This is an old style. I don't have one of those high boxes. It's an old style. Drop French. I have a, and one, and the record on here is, it's kind of warped. Warped.

Well, I'll bet you I have heard it. You know. But. Because I'm quite familiar with it. And I want you. Oh, yes, of course. Yes. Yes. Too busy and wasn't a dream. Yes. Uh-huh. These are very famous records, and take care of this because they've become valuable,
you know. Yes, it's kind of warped like that. And I have several others. So I'd have to find them.
Well, here's a list. Does this look familiar to? Yes. Sweet man.

Sweet George Brown. Lonesome and sorry. Baby of my love. It all depends on you. Ain't you see? My baby I'm a son of that movie. Yeah. That's right. Are you a real sweetheart? Too busy was a dream. Blast night I dreamed. You'd kiss me. Yes. I'm a son of that movie. You're a real sweetheart. Too busy was a dream. Blast night I dreamed. You'd kiss me. Yes. I'm a son of that movie. You're a real sweetheart. Too busy was a dream. Blast night I dreamed. You'd kiss me yesterday.

Now those are some that an Englishman compiled lists of many of the early jays things. And I wanted to ask you about some of them. So it's good we have the list here before us. Did you also record for Vocalion? It seems to me I found Vocalion records. You had heard them? No. Okay. Nobody but the okay.
Oh yes.
That's all.
That's all.
Yes you said that you recorded with Johnny Sincera and they give the date here of March 1926. And then with Jimmy Noon clarinet added a little while later.
Oh yes. He played the clarinet. See.
Was Jimmy working with Johnny or just happened to pick him up to?
I don't think they were working steadily together because Johnny was with an orchestra that played out at the stadium for a long time.
Yes.

And I don't think he worked with Johnny out there because around that time I think maybe Jimmy Noon was working at a place on 35th Street that they called, a nightclub called The Nest I think at that time. See.
That was close to all the other clubs there wasn't it? Between Entertainers and Sunset Summer and that. Was The Nest on the corner do you have to remember?
No it wasn't on the corner it was near the corner of, it was on the north side of 35th Street. Between I think near the corner of Giles I think it was. Between Giles and Prairie I think. I think.
Well now is that the club that became the Apex? I think.
I don't remember them changing the name to the Apex there.

Across the street, second floor across the street from Sunset. They may have. Well. Was a place called the Apex. They may have. But I'm a little uncertain about the location of the bookstore on the Nest. Uh huh. And Apex I'm pretty sure about but I wondered if it might have been the same.
Well it could have been you know because I'm kind of forgetful so it could have been.
Do you remember who was working with Jimmy Noon at that time?

I can't recall who all was working. I think let's see. Let me try to think. Let's see. Who was working with Jimmy Noon. If my husband was here he could tell you better than I because he frequented those places more so than I did. And uh.
Well I wondered if Jerome Carrington might have been playing piano with Jimmy Noon. He may have.
I don't know.

Because soon after Earl Hines came in. Uh. Just about this period Earl Hines uh began playing piano. Previously Glover Comptonized. Yes. But between Compton and Hines. Yeah. I never established who it was. Yeah. Uh huh.
Uh huh. And I can't recall.
Did you know Joe Poston who the alto sax player he might have been with Jimmy Noon.
I know of him. I think Zutti Singleton too.
Zutti Lidas. Very likely. I was playing on the drums. Zutti soon after joined uh probably Carol Dickerson. Probably so. And uh. Yeah.
I. Carol Dickerson I forgot he's passed through. I was on the road with him for a while. Oh were you? With his orchestra.
In what year?

Oh that was in 35. Oh. Uh huh. We traveled through the middle west you know places like uh. Wisconsin, Minnesota and uh Iowa you know places like that. Um. They had uh uh ballroom engagements you know and I was singing. Summer season? Yes. So uh. Very very.
Do you remember anybody in that band? Uh I don't know much about Carol uh. Carol Dickerson? That late. That late.
Well now the man that that's uh the president of the local of the musician's loco. He was with Carol at that time. Oh that's so great.
Yes.
Gray. Gray and his two sons. He had two sons. And uh and uh oh. I can't remember names so well.

Well uh I'll I'll ask Gray about it. Well yes. I uh knew that he had been out earlier. I remember a tour he made with Joe Jordan, some of those things. Yeah. But I uh was unfamiliar with Gray. Well he was with Carol when I was with him.
Yeah.
Tuber or bass? That'd be playing.
I think he was playing the tuba and I think his kids was playing a trumpet you know. I think. Mm hmm. That's right.
Yes. Yes. Okay.
I'll ask him about that.

Mm hmm. And then later uh with uh uh Richard M Jones. Now this sounds as if uh uh possibly this was another date that Johnny Cincere was influential on because he was with you too. Mm hmm. And it says an unknown clarinet. Mm hmm. Do you have any idea who that might have been? This is uh the next spring. Ain't she sweet? And it all depends on you. Richard M Jones, Johnny Cincere.

Yeah. Uh Richard M Jones. I had forgotten all about him. That's true. Richard M Jones. He played piano. Uh huh. And uh let's see. Yeah. I can't think. Who played the clarinet at that time? Well now that I put the question in your mind, it may suddenly bob up two days from now. It might.
Yes. This is something that nobody knows. Yes it did. Could it be Albert Nicklaus?
I had forgotten all about him. I see.
Or Darnell or Stump Evans or. It wasn't Darnell. It wasn't Darnell.
Uh. Or could it be Ralph Brown or uh. Maybe Stump. That name sounds familiar. Stump Evans. It may.
May have been. Stump Evans. It may. May have been. Stump Evans. It may have been. Uh huh. It may have been Stump.
That name sounds very familiar. More so than the others. Well uh. Yeah. The only reason I mention uh. Nicholas is that he played with Richard M Jones but the style of it makes it a little

difficult because uh playing clarinet softly to an accompaniment uh it's not quite as easy to identify the clarinet as if he's playing some sort of. Uh huh. And then a little later again Jimmy Noon and Johnny Sincere they say in December of that year. So every few months why you had a couple sides. Yeah. Coming up didn't you? Then Louie Armstrong finally with Jimmy Noon, Earl Hines, Manson, Manson, Manson, Manson, and Manson. And then Louie Armstrong finally with Jimmy Noon, Earl Hines, Manson, Manson, Manson, Manson, Manson. Uh huh. And then a little later again Jimmy Noon and Johnny Sincere they say in December of that year. So every few months why you had a couple sides. Yeah.
Coming up didn't you?

Then Louie Armstrong finally with Jimmy Noon, Earl Hines, Manson, Manson. Uh huh. Now this was uh. Oh this may have been the summer. No this was after the summer I believe. The summer that Earl Hines joined Jimmy Noon. You know. And Manson Kara happened to be on banjo for that date. Did Johnny Sincere still have something to do with it you think?
No. Uh huh.

This is something that the OK Company came to you about. Yeah. And provided the accompaniment. Was Richard M. Jones the artist's contact man then? He was working for OK Records on and off. Do you remember that he arranged the date for you? Was he present? Possibly not or maybe he would have played piano but they got Earl Hines.
Oh Richard? Who Richard M. Jones?
Yeah. They got Earl Hines. Of course he was acknowledged to be a better piano player.
Well Earl Hines played for me when I played when I was with Louis. You know when I made the records with Louis. Earl was playing then at that time.
Well then there were two other dates. The first one was in June and then on December 11th and December 12th 1928 we played with the same group. Manson Kara then played guitar rather than banjo.

And I had all those records down, you know, and I lost them. I used to live around the corner, you know, 4607 Prairie. And I moved from there here. I've been here 27 years. And I lost quite a bit of it. A lot of music, you know, and a lot of records and things like that.
In the moving, isn't it? Yes, in the moving.
They got misplaced, you know, I mean, repertory, you know, and write-ups and things like that. Oh, that's too bad.
I lost quite a few.

I just got a few. I had a large book of them and now I just got a small, I had two, a large one and a small one, so now I have one. They rented out to clubs now, Club De Lisa. I think a couple of colored fellows leased it and then they, and then they rented out to club, for club dates.

Well, there's even less of that to the club activity than there was about 5, 10 years ago. There used to be a lot of clubs, enough to keep Grand Terrace going and De Lisa and so forth. That's right. Now there's even less of the fraternity and club activity. That's true. I suppose that a great deal of it had gone into churches. stuff

don't you think? Uh-huh. The churches who have taken over that function. Yes. Were you singing in churches when Johnny Sincere heard you, or how did he happen to...? Oh, no. I used to sing around the house all

the time, you know. We always had a lot of company, see, when we were up that way. We had a lot of company, and I'd sing around the house, always somebody to play the piano, you know. Of course, I've been singing all my life. When I was a kid down home, I sang in the Sunday School Choir, you know, and in the Christian Endeavor Choir, see, and sometimes I would help them out. I was, oh, I was about 10 years old, and they'd have me up there in the senior choir, you know. I was, they, my grandmother sang, my mother sang before me. You see, my mother died when I was four, and my daddy died before then, when I was six months old, so I didn't have no sister and brother. I was an orphan, and my maternal grandmother and my mother's brother reared me, see. And they say that she was a singer. I never had no training, but here's where I sang, and went over all right. Uh-huh. Well, it was a voice quality. It was just a natural, just a natural gift, I guess. Uh-huh. So I sing quite a bit down to my church, you know. I don't sing in the choir. What church are you at? I sing Methodist, Greater Walters M. E. Zion, at 3800 Dearborn. Oh, yes. Uh-huh. And I...
The church music today is becoming a very strong matter here on the south side. Once upon a time, it was cabaret music. Today, church music is so outstanding.
Oh, outstanding. They don't have that cabaret music in my church. I don't appreciate that in

the church, anyway. No, well, no. I didn't mean in the church. I meant that as an attraction, uh-huh. The cabaret music showed such uh development over anything that we'd known around Chicago. Yeah. Uh-huh. Today, I think that that the south side churches are leading the way in musical expression. I see. The other churches had uh, used forms and uh, music of uh, oh, century-old,
uh, European. Yeah. And the south side churches have originality. Uh-huh. And

inventiveness and something that's changing the texture of church music greatly. Uh-huh. And, uh, I notice a lot of people come out to hear uh, south side church music on the basis that it's much more vigorous. It's a much more meaningful communication. Yeah. Than the church music that they've heard over
and over. Oh, that's true. That's very true. Mm-hmm. Nothing new to it, nothing uh, stimulating. Uh-huh.

That's right. And uh, so uh, there is a tremendous amount of musical activity here on the south side. I don't know if you know it, but compared with what happens uh, in the rest of town, in the uh, white part of town, there's so little originality. I see. So a little new development. Oh. And uh, we see a sense of daring and adventure and uh, uh, creation. Mm-hmm. That uh, we're just not capable of.

At Samingham. Yeah. Oh, I'm crazy about singing. And at my church, I wish you'd come over to my church, bring your wife sometimes. Oh, they sing so beautiful over there. When do you have musicals over there? Well, now I can't tell just when. Now, uh, they had a Woman's Day affair Sunday before last, while I was on the program. Mm-hmm. Almost every affair they have, they ask me to, to give them a number, you know, and I'm glad to. Well, if they send out a mailing or if,
uh, if you would let us know, I'd be very grateful to you. I'd be so glad to. Yes, I'd be so glad to.

You will appreciate it because they have such lovely singing, lovely singing, every day. And, you know, I'd like for you to come over and bring your wife sometime to our services at 11 o'clock. We don't have, we don't hold them long time like the average colored church. The average colored church will hold them quite, quite late, you know, for 11 o'clock. But always around, well, our services starts about at exactly 11, 10.45. And, uh, quarter to one, we're coming out of there, see. I recorded one the
other day that started about 10, 10.30. Went on toward three o'clock in the afternoon. Oh, no. Just

amazed how long. No, he's my, I passed it. And he's such a wonderful little speaker. You would be, oh, he's so intelligent, you know. He don't have all that old, old-time mess, you know. He's just, just an intelligent speaker. And he just speaks so lovely. And then the choirs we have, we don't have, we used to have a youth choir, but we don't have it anymore. We have, um, the gospel choir and the senior choir. But they sing so beautifully. You would appreciate it so much. You and your wife, too, I think. That was your wife with you, Delvin. I think she's a very sweet person, has a sweet personality.
Well, thank you. You and I agree on that. She's a wonderful girl.
Sweet personality. You tell I say that.
All right, I will. She's glad to learn such opinions, too.
Uh-huh.

Well, just to go back to this story now, we had some dates here. And, uh, did you get any, uh, work as a result of this recording date with Johnny Sincer? And when those records came out, did you, uh, happen to get a job as a result of it? You told me you went to work for Bill Bottoms about a year later.
Yes.
And had you worked, uh, in, uh, in the cafés before that?

No, I hadn't worked in, in the cafés before then. But, um, there was a fellow named, uh, uh, uh, uh. Wait a minute. I'll tell you in just a minute. He belongs to our club. Now, let's see. Uh, uh, uh, but anyway. Oh, my goodness. Why can't I think of that fellow's name? I'm so simple. I'm stupid. I just forget everything. Uh, uh, Clyde, uh, Clyde, Clyde Jenkins. Clyde Jenkins is his name, see. He heard me singing, and he heard the records. And he used to come to our house where we lived up there on, on, uh, Indiana. Uh, so, um, when Bottoms opened that place, he had the orchestra out there, out in, uh, Robbins, Illinois. It was called the Casino Gardens. And so he came for me to, to be in, to sing in the show.
I don't remember, uh, uh, uh, Jenkins as a musician. Clyde Jenkins. What was his instrument? He plays piano. He's still, uh, still active as a piano? He's still, he's still. I mean, he plays.
Yes, he still works someplace on, way out northwest. Oh, so. Yeah, he's still working.
Uh, do you remember anybody else who was with you at, uh, Casino? Uh, the orchestra? Yeah.
No, I don't remember who was in his orchestra. Now, I can't, I have full memory that way.
All right. I, but, but, uh, I, I can get in touch with him. He's probably in the directory of the cheer club.
Oh, yeah, I, I suppose so. He may be. I'll look him up and, and, uh, ask about that.
He should be. He belongs to the, to the cheer club. He's probably in the corner of the choir club.
I'll look up.
Now, this is 60, uh, 61, something. How many pieces did Clyde have at, uh, Garcett's Theater? I think he had, I think he had five.
That's the first thing. He has an address, but he doesn't have a telephone number.
Mm-hmm. All right, I'll wrap him a note. Tell him that I talked with you. And, and I wish he'd call me and see if he had, Langley.
Mm-hmm. 6440 Langley.
And, and, and he's still, uh, playing, is he?
Uh-huh.
Good. Now, uh, there were some vaudeville acts in which the name Jenkins appears. I wonder if he might have been with that. Somebody in Jenkins.
I really couldn't say. I couldn't say. Possibly so. I don't know.
Do you remember what the, what, uh, you did after Casino Gardens?
Well, yes. When I left Casino Gardens, I went to the Panama Cafe. Oh. Yes. Mm-hmm.
Who was there?
Uh, Benny Tallinger was the, was the, uh, boss that run the, Tallinger, run the Panama. Benny Tallinger. Mm-hmm.
Now, is this the 35th? There were people.
That was at 38, I mean, uh, 58th Street.
58th. All right.
Mm-hmm. The Panama, 58th Street. I think it was about three, and the, and the 300 block on 58th Street.
Uh, 300 East.
Mm-hmm.
Yeah. All right.
And, let's see, and, uh, then from there, there was a...
Who was with you at Panama as a musical accompaniment? Do you remember the orchestra or your pianist?

Now, uh, the pianist was, uh, Jerry Wilson. He used to make all my orchestrate, arrange all my orchestrations for me. Jerry Wilson was a pianist, like, you know, pianist. And I don't know who all was in his orchestra. I can't think.
Two or three pieces?
Oh, they must have had four or fives, because that was a pretty good, pretty good-sized nightclub. Mm-hmm.
Did you, uh, uh, perform as a, uh, uh, uh, nightclub act, or were you a singer?
Just a singer. A singer with a band? Single, single, single. In the show. In the show.
Uh-huh. All right. That's what I meant.
Mm-hmm.
In the Panama show. Do you remember any other, uh, performers who, uh, appeared at the Panama while you were there?
Yeah, Marie Claybrook, she was there, and, and, uh, uh, Nadine Douglas. Jimmy White. He, he was, uh, Jimmy White. He was the, uh, producer of the show. Uh-huh.
Well, you said about 27 at Casino. Was it the next year at Panama, would you say?

Well, I tell you, after, that wasn't directly after I left the casino that I went. See, when I, after I quit there, I didn't work no more until about, in the nightclubs anymore until about, about, uh, let's see, what year was it I started back? That was 27. I didn't start back anymore until about 34, I guess.
Is that so? It was, uh, well into the depression before you, uh,

Yeah. Back in that kind of work. Yeah. Correct. By 34, cause that's, that's, uh, that's back when I went to the Panama, see, when, uh-huh. I didn't go, I didn't go directly back. I quit. And, uh, this piano, it has history behind it. Everybody that came to Chicago played on this piano. Duke, we had a little tea room around the corner when we lived around there during the depression. And, uh, Duke Ellington, Earl Hines, all the performers that came to Chicago at that time came to our place. At one time, uh, some colored fellow friend of ours brought a part of Dan Garber's orchestra out. He and, see, we'd serve chicken and steaks. Oh, yeah. And, of course, the gin on the side, you know. So, uh-
This was the place on Indiana Avenue?
No. When we lived at 4607 Prairie in our house.
Oh, yeah.

In our house. And we, this piano, my husband says, it's too bad that we didn't have, get all the autographs from the, from the famous people that played on this piano. It's still good, and it's 33 years old. And, uh- Do you play yourself? No, I don't. I, I used to play a lot, but I had an accident on a glass door.
Yes, yes.

Cut, all my leaders was cut on a glass door, even to the sun. Yeah. So, I lost the execution, you know. Right now. I can't execute. Uh-huh. But I can just pick it out enough to, uh, learn my songs. I can learn my songs. I don't have to have nobody teach me that.
Yes, yes, the functionality. I, I see.
Uh-huh. But I used to play pretty good before that happened.
Uh, after Panama, where did, where did you go?
Oh, after Panama, I went to, there was another nightclub in the 200 block on 58th street called the Golden Pheasant.
Yes.

된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된된
Then? Do you remember anybody there? I can remember Bill Thrillkill and Chick Bailey, she's a girl she's passed on to. Was she also a singer?
Yes, she was a singer. What did Thrillkill do?
He was a singer. Well, I can't remember who all was there.
The orchestra?

Let's see who had the orchestra there. I think, uh... Almond Ellison, I think. His passed too. Almond Ellison. I think, I think he had it then. But it's been so long, you know, things have, you know, just...
We'll try to locate because maybe they advertised in the Defender someplace, did they? And we could go hunting through those files.

Yes, I, that's what I was looking for that book. I thought it was, I thought it was up front, but I got it put away someplace. I don't know where it is. I'll, I'll have it sometime, maybe next time you're around any place, you know, that I know you're gonna be somewhere. I'll find it and bring it maybe. And, uh, then from there I went to, uh, Clefter Lisa.
Mm-hmm. All right. So, uh, that was over a period of about two years, from 34 to... Delbert Bright.
Delbert Bright, yeah. Uh-huh. I think he had...
Delbert Bright had been in the band at the, uh... At the Club de Lisa.
Club de Lisa when you started. Yeah. Delbert Bright. Mm-hmm.
Well, Delbert Bright had been in Albert Hammond's band, and, uh, Albert was, uh, had left and was over at the Etcler. Mm-hmm. Or something of the sort about that time around the corner from... Yeah.
And then he was, it wasn't long before, um... Saunders. Red, Red Saunders came in. Mm-hmm. Mm-hmm.

Uh, let's see, uh, Delbert Bright might have had that, uh, uh, did, uh, did, uh, Jimmy Hoskins stay on playing drums? If you haven't remembered him, Little Pella. Uh, and, uh, Ike Perkins guitar? Ike was there.
Mm-hmm.
Um, and a small trumpet player whose name I don't remember. Yeah, I, I forget his name, but...
I remember, I can see him now, but I, I forget his name. Hi, Daddy.

Uh, let's see. No, I, I wouldn't have it, I, I would have it in, uh, in one of the other volumes. It has Albert's group. Uh, I think he was a, uh, a boy from New Orleans. Do you happen to recall that, what the trumpet player was? Mm-hmm. I can't, I can't, uh, be awfully sure, so... Mm-hmm. Well, you said you were, uh, at the, uh, Delisa in and out, uh, a few weeks or a few months at a time?
Yeah, I, uh, well, when I went there, I, I stayed there about a year, kind of a couple of months or something like that. I'd say about 14 or 16 months straight I stayed there. Mm-hmm.
That was your first time, uh, for 14, 16 months?
Uh-huh. Then, when I left there, I went to, to where I worked at the, uh, Cotton Club for a while. Uh, which one? Uh, uh, uh, on Blue Island. Yes. Over there. And, uh...
Do you remember who, uh, had the band there then?
I'm trying to think now, who had the band. Thaymond Hayes? He may have. You get put that...
A band from, from, uh, St. Louis? Or a Chicago band? Or there was also a Chicago band, but I don't remember whose it was. Mm-hmm.
I forgot. I'd forgotten. Who, who was that? I didn't, I didn't stay there very long. Mm-hmm. On Blue Island. Then I... I worked for Jim Martin.
Where was he? 1900 Westlake.
A little before Western. The Martin's Corners, as well as the following. 1900 Westlake. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Uh-huh. Westlake. Do you remember who was, uh, the music over there?
Now, uh... Where was he?
1900 Westlake. 1900 Westlake.

Oh, yes, of course. Yes, uh, just, just beyond, uh, was that West... no. A little before Western. The Martin's Corners, as well as the following. 1900 Westlake. Uh-huh. Do you remember who was, uh, the music over there? Now, um... Shorty McConnell was over there for a while, was it? The little trumpet player, was it?
Yeah. A little before Western. The Martin's Corners, as well as the following.
1900 Westlake. Uh-huh. Do you remember who was, uh, the music over there?
Now, um...
Shorty McConnell was over there for a while, was it? The little trumpet player, very short.
He may have been there then. Because, you see, I can't just remember in my head, and I had, had to be put down, and
I lost it, you know. Were you singing, uh, in the show also?
Singing, in the show, always in the show, in these nightclubs, see. Then when I left there, I went to the 50-100 Club. Okay.
What's happened to Jim Martin? Do you know?
